title: UPDATE Statement & Multi-Table Joins
description: Update records efficiently, mutate columns based on other tables using UPDATE ... FROM, and retrieve modified rows with RETURNING.

data.text: The **`UPDATE`** statement modifies existing column values in a table. In PostgreSQL, updates can reference columns from other tables using the non-standard but extremely useful **`UPDATE ... FROM`** syntax.

data.title: Applying Tiered Discounts from Pricing Table
data.content: Updates product prices based on category discount rules.
data.code:
UPDATE products p
SET price = p.price * (1 - c.discount_rate)
FROM categories c
WHERE p.category_id = c.id
  AND c.discount_rate > 0
RETURNING p.id, p.title, p.price;

data.title: HOT (Heap-Only Tuples) Updates
data.text: In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE writes a new version of the row tuple (MVCC). If the updated columns are not indexed and there is space in the original heap page, PostgreSQL performs a **Heap-Only Tuple (HOT)** update, avoiding the massive cost of rewriting index pointers!

`UPDATE ... RETURNING` gives you the new values in the same statement, which removes a follow-up SELECT and the race condition that comes with it. You can also wrap the update in a CTE to use the changed rows in a second step.

data.title: Return updated values and chain them in a CTE
data.content: The first statement returns the new balance; the second raises prices and then sorts the changed rows in one round trip.
data.code:
-- Return the new balance directly
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE id = 42
RETURNING id, balance;

-- Update and use the results in a second step
WITH changed AS (
    UPDATE products
    SET price = price * 1.10
    WHERE category = 'electronics'
    RETURNING sku, price
)
SELECT sku, price
FROM changed
ORDER BY price DESC;

data.title: Updates create new row versions
data.text: PostgreSQL MVCC writes a new tuple for every update. If the changed column is not indexed and the page has free space, it is a HOT update and the indexes are not touched. Updating an indexed column or a column referenced by a foreign key forces index maintenance and often triggers a new heap page, which causes bloat over time. VACUUM reclaims that space, but the write amplification is real.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Always include a `WHERE` clause in `UPDATE` to avoid modifying every row in the table.
Use `UPDATE ... FROM` to join other tables during mutation.
Avoid updating indexed columns unnecessarily to maximize HOT update optimization.
